Japan’s wave of corporate breaches is the latest sign that AI is changing how hacking works.

Since Sept 25, 18 Japanese companies have disclosed breaches, including Tokyo Metro, Japan Post, Lawson, Nikkei, Yamato and Sagawa. Attackers got about 6.6M Times Car accounts, some with driver’s license images. Burger King Japan says 11.18M app member records were affected, and Sourcenext says up to 22.5M records may be out.

Last week, JPCERT/CC, the country’s national computer emergency response team, posted its findings from the investigations into these breaches. The attackers used AI to scan for known vulnerabilities and to attack companies’ APIs. Often they did this by pulling apart a company’s Android app to find the endpoints and any keys left in the code. It is also no surprise that Japanese companies are particularly vulnerable. Japan is still catching up on basic digitization, with many offices still using fax machines to this day! 

Now even the PM is getting involved, urging anyone running a PHP website to patch two critical vulnerabilities immediately, or temporarily take the site offline if they can't.

No matter what poverty line you choose, the share of the global population below it has declined.

The World Bank's International Poverty Line is an extremely low poverty line. Set at $3 per day, it draws attention to the living conditions of the poorest people on the planet.

In the chart above, you can see how the share below this poverty line has declined over the last generation. In the year 2000, 36% of the world’s population lived on less than $3 per day. In 2024, it was 10%.

But is progress against global poverty only happening when measured against such a very low poverty line?

The chart gives the answer. The entire blue line is below the entire dark red line. This tells us that no matter what line you choose, the share below it has declined globally.

Progress against higher poverty lines has been large, too. The share living on less than $5 a day has declined from 57% to 25%, and the share living on less than $10 a day has declined from 74% to 53%.

But on the right-hand side of the chart, we see that most people still live on low incomes: 81% of people in the world live on less than $30 a day, or about $900 a month.

(written by @MaxCRoser)

Today is the birthday of Clinton Joseph Davisson, the Nobel Prize-winning American physicist who discovered electron diffraction. In an experiment conducted with physicist Lester Germer, Davisson showed that, when directed at a crystal, an electron beam will produce a diffraction pattern with wave-like attributes. The Davisson-Germer experiment confirmed a similar hypothesis proposed in 1924 by Louis de Broglie, with Davisson and Lester becoming the first to demonstrate the wave properties of the electron.

Their Nobel Prize-winning work proved the principle of wave-particle duality, which states that every elementary particle or quantic entity exhibits properties, not only of particles, but also waves.

DSX POD: $IREN’s Path to Rapid Compute Deployment Is Now Crystal Clear

I still have saved on my computer the discussion between IREN COO Kent and a Lenovo vice president in March this year, as well as the discussion with NVIDIA representatives in September. Both covered the collaboration and interaction among the parties on GPU cluster racks, cluster cabling, network topology, and commissioning. With NVIDIA’s launch yesterday of the new containerized DSX POD cluster at GTC Berlin, the mystery behind many of IREN’s moves over the past year has finally been unraveled. Its path to rapid compute deployment has now become crystal clear.

DSX POD is a standardized, factory-preintegrated modular unit designed by NVIDIA for AI factories. It fully integrates compute, networking, storage, power, and liquid cooling within a container, with cabling completed and the system validated before leaving the factory. Once delivered on-site, it can be connected directly to power, cooling, and networking. This reduces deployment time from the traditional six months to approximately 14 days, dramatically simplifying on-site complexity and accelerating the production of the first token.

An AI factory designed to work with DSX POD only needs to establish unified planning, energy and liquid-cooling infrastructure, data-center-grade network backbones, scheduling systems for training and inference, and standardized security and operations. Once the PODs arrive, the facility can then be brought online rapidly through a plug-and-play process. The core concept is to treat the entire campus as a continuous compute production line: PODs serve as modular capacity units at the front end, while software-defined resource orchestration at the back end closes the loop between training, inference, and deployment. This enables the entire factory to produce intelligence reliably and consistently.

This dramatically accelerates AI factory construction and ensures that high-quality compute capacity can come online faster. The most difficult and quality-sensitive components have been standardized and modularized. An AI factory only needs to get environmental approvals, network cabling, power supply, and external cooling interfaces right to begin producing tokens rapidly. This resolves several of the major bottlenecks in bringing compute capacity online.

Once DSX POD encapsulates the most complex, error-prone, and specialist-dependent stages of the process, the pace of AI factory construction shifts, for the first time, from an engineering-cycle model to a supply-chain-cycle model. The repeated commissioning, rework, and inconsistent interfaces among different contractors that characterized the old approach are compressed into a standardized module validated at the factory. The areas where an AI factory must truly concentrate its efforts are environmental approvals, power, networking, and cooling—all priorities that IREN is particularly good at executing and has always placed at the forefront.

As a result, the pace of compute deployment no longer depends primarily on the experience of engineering teams, but on whether the campus can provide a stable supply of energy and cooling. Once a POD arrives, connects to power and liquid cooling, and links to the network, the entire cluster can be brought online within days. Training workloads can immediately be scheduled, and token production capacity can ramp up like an assembly line. The biggest bottlenecks that previously constrained AI factory expansion—slow construction, inconsistent quality, and unpredictable deployment schedules—are removed from the system. For the first time, AI factories have the potential to achieve the kind of scalable replication long established in manufacturing.

At this GTC, NVIDIA announced four partners in its DSX ecosystem: IREN, Nebius, Lambda, and Nscale. Each has a different area of emphasis in its collaboration with NVIDIA.

IREN: Industrial-scale deployment at gigawatt scale

IREN is taking DSX POD beyond a standardized module and turning it into an industrialized production line at gigawatt scale. With its own power resources, substations, and zero-water-consumption liquid-cooling system, IREN is integrating PODs into gigawatt-scale campuses as replicable units of productive capacity. This is the first time DSX is being translated from an architectural concept into a real-world template for super-scale AI factories.

NEBIUS: Sovereign AI

Nebius is less focused on scale and more focused on sovereignty. AI compute development in Europe is constrained by geopolitics, regulatory compliance, and data sovereignty requirements. Nebius uses DSX to build sovereign AI clouds on European soil that can be regulated, audited, and hosted locally. This allows European enterprises and governments to access high-performance clusters within their own jurisdictions, demonstrating the replicability of DSX across different regions and regulatory environments.

NSCALE: Pushing energy efficiency to its limits

Nscale focuses on maximizing energy efficiency. In Iceland’s extremely cold environment, it uses DSX MaxLPS to maximize inference output from every watt of power. Under a fixed power budget of 264 kW, it increased throughput by 49%, demonstrating that DSX is not only capable of supporting large-scale deployments but can also substantially increase compute density under extreme power constraints. This is an important validation of DSX from an energy-efficiency perspective.

LAMBDA: The developer ecosystem

Lambda focuses on the developer ecosystem, deploying DSX MaxLPS in a bare-metal cloud environment to validate throughput improvements under real-world developer workloads. In tests using the B200 architecture, it achieved a 24% increase in token throughput and a 19% increase in GPU capacity under the same power budget. This demonstrates that DSX can improve resource efficiency in cloud environments, rather than merely optimizing data-center engineering.

Looking at the overall strategic weight of these partnerships, IREN occupies the most central position. It is responsible for the heaviest, most difficult, and most consequential part of the DSX industrial system: taking DSX POD from a standardized module into a real industrial environment at gigawatt scale, integrating the most complex infrastructure elements, including power, liquid cooling, substations, and flexible power response, and transforming DSX from a technical solution into a mass-deployable template for super-scale AI factories.

By comparison, Nebius validates sovereign and regulatory-compliance scenarios, Nscale validates the limits of energy efficiency, and Lambda validates the developer ecosystem. All are important, but each addresses a particular dimension of DSX. IREN, by contrast, is validating DSX itself as an industrial system: large-scale deployment, heavy infrastructure investment, and continuous productive capacity. That is why IREN carries the greatest weight in any comprehensive assessment of the ecosystem.

This also makes IREN’s compute deployment roadmap much clearer. According to Jensen Huang, DSX POD can accelerate the deployment of compute capacity. For a gigawatt-scale compute campus, it can bring capacity online a quarter earlier, generating $10 billion in cash flow sooner and dramatically improving project economics. For a company like IREN, with multiple gigawatt-scale campuses, the implications are enormous. It also immediately widens IREN’s competitive advantage over Nebius.

Before DSX POD was unveiled at GTC Berlin, Nebius’s central differentiating narrative was its ability to design its own racks and independently handle cluster cabling, network topology, commissioning, and full-system stress testing. The market had come to regard this end-to-end, on-site cluster integration capability as one of Nebius’s important competitive moats. In comparisons with IREN, quite a few analysts argued that IREN relied on ODMs such as Dell and Lenovo for cluster integration and was therefore relatively weak in underlying hardware engineering, while Nebius enjoyed greater technological autonomy thanks to its in-house cluster capabilities.

The launch of DSX POD directly rewrites this competitive benchmark.

These prefabricated containerized units have their GPU racks assembled, high-speed NVLink cabling installed, Spectrum-X networking deployed, and full-system burn-in and stress testing completed inside ODM factories. Cluster integration and low-level tuning—tasks that previously required substantial engineering expertise and formed a key part of Nebius’s differentiation—have become standardized, commercialized deliverables.

As long as an operator has a campus infrastructure platform that meets DSX specifications, it can receive a POD, connect it to power and cooling, and bring the cluster online rapidly.

This does not mean Nebius’s technology has become irrelevant. Rather, the basis of its former competitive moat has been reset. NVIDIA’s ecosystem positioning shifts Nebius’s differentiation toward the upper layers of the stack: physical AI workbenches, simulation, and agent development environments, rather than making underlying cluster engineering its primary competitive battleground.

Nevertheless, losing this underlying source of differentiation still has a substantial impact, because the economic consequences are significant. Last week, a Nebius supporter who debated me still regarded this capability as a moat and argued that it gave Nebius superior economics. But when speed, time, reliability, standardization, and scalability are taken into account, the economic advantage of doing everything independently becomes almost negligible. Indeed, IREN’s engineering capabilities in integrating the entire infrastructure platform could give it a substantial first-mover advantage and additional economic benefits.

This is a classic example of why going it alone can be inferior to bringing together the strongest capabilities across an entire industry.

IREN had already established a partnership with Dell when it first went public. As it moved deeper into the AI industry, its collaborations with NVIDIA and Lenovo also became increasingly extensive. This allowed IREN to understand the industry's key development pathways and emerging trends earlier.

The launch of DSX POD also helps explain many of IREN’s seemingly slow moves over the past year. The redevelopment of its Canadian campuses and the demolition and reconstruction of the original data center in Childress may well be related to DSX POD. Even if these projects do not immediately need to conform to the standardized interfaces, understanding the direction in which the industry is moving allows IREN to prepare in advance.

Before this system was introduced, IREN was capable of delivering AI factories at a rate of 50 MW per month. With this critical module now standardized, the interfaces for the various components of the supporting AI factory infrastructure should also become standardized relatively quickly. IREN is one of the key players responsible for this work.

Judging from this trajectory, IREN could soon substantially increase its AI factory delivery rate to 100 MW or even 150 MW per month. For a company like IREN, with abundant power resources secured, the implications of rapidly scaling deployment are enormous.

It would also accelerate the cash-generation flywheel, enabling faster payback on both GPUs and data centers and addressing the market’s biggest current concern: whether the returns on such substantial investments will be sufficient.

As for whether the recent sell-off in IREN amounts to selling gold at a bargain price, I will leave that judgment to each of you.

$PRME One of the aspects I like most about Prime's platform is the modularity and how it positions them to capitalize on recent FDA efforts to streamline approvals and make bespoke genetic medicine more scalable.

Although prime editing can theoretically repair most genetic mutations, old FDA rules would treat every new guide RNA as a brand-new drug. Spending years and tens of millions of dollars repeating animal tox, biodistribution, and manufacturing validation for single point mutations left thousands of rare diseases commercially stranded. 

In light of ongoing shifts at the FDA, Prime is well positioned to break through this bottleneck:

1) Turning Drug Development into an Interchangeable Process

Prime’s Universal Liver LNP packages five standardized chemical components around prime editor mRNA.

• To target a new liver mutation or disease, Prime leaves the entire nanoparticle shell, delivery formulation, and editor mRNA completely intact, swapping only the guide RNA sequences (less than 5% of the drug’s total mass).

• Under the FDA’s Platform Technology Designation and Leveraging Prior Knowledge frameworks, Prime could cross-reference safety, stability, and CMC data across programs. This is likely why PM647 (AATD) cleared its IND in September 2026 just weeks after PM577a (Wilson disease) in July, cutting preclinical time and capital expenditure with each successive pipeline asset.

2) "Umbrella" Approvals Across Mutational Families

In Wilson disease, Prime’s lead in vivo candidate (PM577a) targets the H1069Q mutation common in the West, while a follow-on candidate addresses the R778L variant prevalent in East Asia.

• Under the FDA’s draft Plausible Mechanism Framework, once PM577a demonstrates clinical proof-of-mechanism in the human liver, Prime could potentially bundle follow-on ATP7B guides into master protocols or supplemental filings without running multi-year, standalone trials for every variant.

• As CEO Dr. Allan Reine noted after dosing the first PM577a patient this month, the same shared LNP delivery approach provides a direct path to expand into global patient populations across mutational families.

3) De-Risked Human Biology & Near-Term Catalysts

Prime editing is no longer purely theoretical. In PM359 for p47phox CGD, Prime proved in humans (NEJM, Dec 2025) that prime editors repair DNA cleanly without double-stranded breaks, restoring functional neutrophil activity to 69–83% (well clear of the 20% clinical efficacy threshold).

• Holding RMAT and Rare Pediatric Disease designations, PM359 is on track for a streamlined 1H 2027 BLA under the FDA's Rare Disease Evidence Principles (RDEP), a milestone that could unlock a Priority Review Voucher (PRV) worth about $100M+ in non-dilutive capital.

• Upcoming 2027 clinical readouts for PM577a (Wilson) and PM647 (AATD) rely on direct, objective biomarkers (serum ceruloplasmin, 64Cu PET copper efflux, and functional M-AAT protein), insulating the platform from the subjective clinical-scale failures that tripped up others.

In short, the modular nature of Prime's platform combined with the FDA's regulatory updates could allow the tech to evolve from an unscalable trial-and-error grind into a plug-and-play platform, sharply lowering the cost and latency required to commercialize genetic cures.
